belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

The first part of Define is the business case. Here's what it is and why it matters: The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It earns the project its support, and it’s the first thing the Define report shows — people outside the team only back what they can understand and size.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves time and resources by describing what is wrong, where and since when, its scale, and its cost.
reply.example:
Sample only — to show the form of a good answer. Do not copy it; answer for your own process.
During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month.
reply.prompt: Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.

belt: Across our three hospital sites, 23% of supplier invoices were paid after their 30-day terms from January to June 2026. Late payments to our suppliers are costing us: we paid about £62,000 in late-payment interest and lost early-payment discounts last year, and three key medical suppliers put us on stop twice this year, which held up ward stock.

reply.answer:
Your business case is starting to take shape, but it’s missing one key detail: the baseline measurement. To meet the acceptance criteria, the business case needs a specific baseline figure, such as the total number of invoices or the total number of late payments during the stated period. Without this, we can’t fully understand the scale of the issue.

For example, if you know how many invoices were processed in total from January to June 2026, and how many of those were late, we can calculate the actual number of late payments and use that as your baseline measurement. This will make your business case more precise and actionable.

Can you provide the total number of invoices or late payments for that time period?
reply.explanation: The business case identifies the problem, where and when it occurs, its size today, and its cost. It earns the project its support.

**What it is:** The project team: who leads, who sponsors, who owns the process, and who does the work — each with a name, a role and what they will do.

**Why it matters:** A project needs people before it needs work. The champion clears obstacles and the process owner keeps the result after the project ends; without them a good fix fades.

**Illustration:** "Leader: Anna (Green Belt, runs the project). Champion: Mark, Finance Director (approves, removes blockers). Process owner: Jo, Billing Manager (owns the process). reply.answer:
Welcome to Measure. Quick recap of what Define locked in, so we're building on the same picture:

• **Problem:** From January to June 2026, 23% of supplier invoices across our three hospital sites were paid after their 30-day terms. Late payments led to suppliers chasing the accounts payable team by phone and email, and some putting us on stop — holding ward stock. This caused interest charges, lost discounts, and supplier stops, with delays happening at the "Resolve mismatches" and "Approve invoices" steps.
• **Baseline:** One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.
• **Target:** Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.
• **Process (SIPOC):** Invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites. Outputs: paid invoices and remittance advice. Customers: the suppliers, and our ward managers who rely on their deliveries. Metrics: days from invoice receipt to payment release, and the share of invoices with a match exception.

Now, what Measure actually does: we expand that SIPOC into a detailed process map, decide what to collect and how, check the measurement itself can be trusted, confirm the process is behaving consistently, establish a real baseline, and prioritise which inputs are most likely driving the problem. You don't need to hold these in a fixed order in your head — I'll guide you — but here's the full menu so nothing's a surprise:

**Required (7)**
□ Detailed process map — timings, people, value vs waste per step
□ Data collection plan — what, how much, how often, who
□ Stability check — is the process behaving consistently?
□ Baseline — the current level, once we trust the data
□ Cause prioritisation — scoring what might be driving it
□ Vital few X's — the shortlist Analyse will test
□ Issues and barriers — what's in your way

**Recommended (3)**
□ Sigma level · □ Measurement system check · □ Secondary metrics

**Progress: 0 of 7 required complete**

We'll work through these roughly in the order above, and I'll flag the two recommended ones — the measurement system check and the sigma level — when we reach them, rather than saving them for the end. First up: expanding your Define map, because everything else attaches to it. Let me show you what that looks like.

To add detail: this is based on the AP ledger for January to June 2026, across all three hospital sites, and the finance director has agreed it.

define_structured.voc_summary: Our customers are the suppliers, who need paying on the agreed 30-day terms, and our own ward managers, who need stock to keep arriving. Suppliers complain most about payments arriving late, not knowing when they will be paid, and being unable to see the status of an invoice once it is submitted. Ward managers complain most about deliveries being held.
define_structured.problem_statement: From January to June 2026, 23% of supplier invoices across our three hospital sites were paid after their 30-day terms. Late payments led to suppliers chasing the accounts payable team by phone and email, and some putting us on stop — holding ward stock. This caused interest charges, lost discounts, and supplier stops, with delays happening at the "Resolve mismatches" and "Approve invoices" steps.

baseline_estimate.raw: One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.

project_scope.in_scope: Invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites.
project_scope.out_scope: Non-PO invoices, payroll, procurement tendering, and the ERP system itself.

define_structured.goal_statement: Reduce the late payment rate from 23% to under 5% by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.

target_value.raw: Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices.

define_structured.target_date: We plan to finish the project by 31 March 2027 (2027-03-31).

benefits_analysis.cost_of_gap: £68,000 a year in interest and lost discounts, from the savings calculation.
benefits_analysis.realisation_schedule: Starts in Q2 2027 at about £17,000 a quarter.

define_structured.secondary_metrics: Two things must not get worse: the number of supplier payment queries the AP team handles each month, and AP staff overtime hours. Both should stay at or below today's levels.
